To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the carbon footprints are not just a matter of the individual choices, but are also tied to the form and structure of the urbanization; (ii) the carbon footprint is a product of a complex interplay of many different consumption activities and their economies-of-scale effects; and (iii) the lifestyles of the middle income consumers are surprisingly stable and do not vary much when the budget constraints of the individuals are the same.
the carbon footprints of the middle-income residents of Finland vary little due to the complementary effects of the lifestyles.

(i) the carbon footprints of the middle-income households in the four area types are similar, (ii) the footprints of the less urbanized households would be lower if the economies-of-scale effects would be taken into account, and (iii) motorization increases the footprint significantly, but housing type has little effect on the footprint.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between urban form, lifestyles and GHG emissions.

how urbanization, lifestyles and GHG emissions are intertwined, and the results of this study suggest that the relationship between urban form, lifestyles and GHGs should be further investigated in the future.
the relationship between the urban form, lifestyles, and the GHG emissions.

urban form has only a limited impact on lifestyles and GHG emissions, and that the most significant factors are the income level and the size of the household.
the urban form does not matter much for GHG emissions, but the lifestyle of the individual does.
the GHG emissions of the middle-class are mainly determined by the size of the household and the income level.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the urban form is an important factor in the GHG emissions but the impacts are not as straightforward as previously thought.
the urban form has a significant impact on the carbon footprint of the middle-income households in Finland, but the impact is not as straightforward as the prevailing paradigm suggests.
a compact city form does not necessarily lead to a compact lifestyle and, consequently, to lower GHG emissions.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the GHG emissions of urban residents should be assessed in a comprehensive manner, and the lifestyles of the residents should not be considered as a product of their values alone but rather as situated in their urban environment.
the GHG impacts of urbanization cannot be reduced into a single indicator such as density or housing energy consumption.
the lifestyles are situated and that the GHG assessment of urban forms should include a wide range of consumption activities.
